meta.title: Vector — k-nearest over a stored column, every way it runs
meta.description: One k-nearest query over a derive: 'vector' column measured every physical way it can run — the resident sweep with no database, the shipped plan, its own statement by hand, ORDER BY over a registered function, the same query with no column at all, and sqlite-vec — equivalence-gated, with what the column costs to write and to store, and the brute-force ceiling as numbers.

notes: the row the column exists to beat: at 10,000 × 768 the same query document over a collection with no vector column costs 14.47× the k-nearest plan

the row the database cannot win: the k-nearest plan is 6.87× the resident sweep over a Float32 matrix at 50,000 × 768 — that sweep starts from decoded floats in RAM and pays nothing for durability, filters or a process that can restart
the plan costs 1.07× its own statement run by hand, which is what the cut, the engine re-rank and the winners fetch add over fetch-and-sweep

pushing the rank into SQL, re-measured against the real column: ORDER BY over a registered function is 0.90× the fetch-and-rank at 50,000 × 768 (0.90–0.94× across the grid), so it is at rough parity on speed. The plan still does not emit it, and after this measurement the reasons are not speed: bun's SQLite binding has no user-function API at all, so a plan that needed one would exclude an executor; and an ORDER BY over the column's own score decides the order in SQL, where the engine — the only party that can see the document's secondary keys — has to decide it for the three executors to agree on ties

the column costs 2.06× the write; its bytes are 0.18× the documents' own and the database measures 1.20× as large. Packed, one vector is 5.25× smaller than the same vector as JSON in the document beside it
sqlite-vec answers the same probes 5.56× faster than the plan at 50,000 × 768, out of a database 6.59× smaller that holds the vectors and no documents

the ceiling, measured: the plan scans at 5.2 ns per vector component, so one query reaches 100 ms at about 24,000 vectors of 768 dimensions and one second at about 249,000. Past that this design is the wrong tool: exact brute force is linear in n·d and no margin changes that. sqlite-vec's cost is linear in the same product on this build (0.915 ns per component, one second at about 1,423,000 vectors), so what lies past the ceiling is an approximate index that neither of these rows is

headline.title: k-nearest over a stored vector column: 194.89 ms for the top 10 of 50,000 × 768
headline.text: The k-nearest plan — the column cuts the candidates, the engine orders them, the winners' documents are fetched — answers 50,000 × 768 in 194.89 ms. The same query document over a collection with no vector column costs 14.47× that at 10,000 × 768, which is the row the column exists to beat. The row it cannot beat is the one with no database in it: the same top-10 over a resident Float32 matrix is 28.37 ms, 6.87× faster, starting from decoded floats in RAM and paying nothing for durability, filters or a process that can restart. Pushing the rank into SQL — ORDER BY over a registered function — measures 0.90–0.94× the fetch-and-rank across the grid, which is close enough that the reason the plan does not emit it is portability and tie correctness rather than speed: bun has no user-function API, and only the engine can break a tie by the document's own keys. The column is not free: it costs 2.06× the write and its bytes are 0.18× the documents' own. sqlite-vec, the extension built for this, answers the same probes 5.56× faster out of a database 6.59× smaller that holds no documents — and it is a native extension, which is the thing this store does not require. The ceiling is arithmetic, not opinion: at 5.2 ns per vector component one query reaches one second at about 249,000 vectors of 768 dimensions, and past that an exact brute-force scan is the wrong tool.

tables.note: Lower is better. Every path answered the identical top-k on every probe before it was timed. The resident sweep starts from decoded floats in RAM and pays nothing for durability, where every SQLite path starts from bytes on a page — it is the row the database has to be worth, not a row it can win. The JSON-doc row is what a collection without the column still runs, measured up to 10,000 documents. sqlite-vec holds the same bytes in a vec0 table that carries no documents, so its probe reads far fewer pages than a fetch over the collection — the storage table below is how much less it stores.

tables.note: The column costs a JSON round trip of the member plus an l2-normalize and a pack on every write. A suite that published only queries would leave this out, and a consumer choosing the column has to see it beside what the query saves. The rival column inserts the same packed bytes into its own table and stores no document at all.

head: leg

tables.note: The first two columns are payload — the bytes those columns hold, summed. The next two are what the database costs: pages allocated, read from the connection. They answer different questions, and they can disagree: a column whose bytes fit in slack SQLite was already leaving on the page costs nothing until they do not. One 768-dimension vector is 3,072 bytes packed against 16,141 as a JSON number array inside the document it is derived from — the document carries the vector either way, which is why the column adds bytes rather than replacing them. The rival's database holds the vectors and nothing else.
